## How it works

- [statement] A critical review concluded that epidemiology alone makes causal attribution difficult because relevant exposures may precede manifest PD by decades; complementary experimental evidence increases causal plausibility. Observational associations should retain this qualification. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11832802/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] A 2025 modelling study using GBD 2021 projected 25.2 million people with PD worldwide in 2050 (95% uncertainty interval 21.7–30.1 million), a 112% increase from 2021; these are forecasts, not observed future counts. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-03-05) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11881235/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] The paraquat evidence has conflicting interpretations: Tanner and colleagues’ 2011 Agricultural Health Study nested case-control analysis reported an association with PD (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7); EPA’s page updated November 3, 2026 states that it has not found a clear link between labeled paraquat uses and PD. The regulatory statement is qualified by labeled-use conditions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-03) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution · also: https://www.epa.gov/ingredients-used-pesticide-products/paraquat-dichloride
- [statement] A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis (databases searched up to May 2019) found, across nine case-control studies, that PD occurrence was 25% higher in participants exposed to paraquat, while the only cohort investigation included showed a non-significant OR of 1.08; the authors concluded that the data indicate a positive association but that the weight-of-evidence does not enable one to assume an indisputable cause-effect relationship. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31476981/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] Tanner et al. reported an association between paraquat use and PD in FAME (110 cases, 358 controls; OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7), whereas the later AHS prospective analysis reported no statistically clear association (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.84–1.41). These overlapping study populations and different designs should not be counted as independent replications. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7822498/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The Camp Lejeune result cannot uniquely attribute the association to TCE: exposure was inferred from residence, diagnostic data were limited to VHA/Medicare users, and PCE, vinyl chloride, benzene or mixtures could have contributed. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10186205/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] Air-pollution findings differ across settings: a Taiwan nationwide study reported positive associations for several pollutants that persisted in multipollutant models, while a Northern Ireland study found no overall association for medium-term PM₂.₅ or NO2 exposure and medication-defined PD onset; its under-50 subgroup showed a PM₂.₅ association. These exposure windows and outcome definitions limit direct comparison. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12322442/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12521372/
- [statement] The same Global Burden of Disease analysis reported male-to-female ratios of age-standardised prevalence rates of 1·40 (95% UI 1·36-1·43) in 2016 and 1·37 (1·34-1·40) in 1990, and estimated 211 296 deaths (95% UI 167 771-265 160) due to Parkinson's disease in 2016. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30287051/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] The Global Burden of Disease investigators concluded that the global burden of Parkinson's disease more than doubled over the past generation as a result of increasing numbers of older people, with potential contributions from longer disease duration and environmental factors. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30287051/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] A 2023 narrative review in J Parkinsons Dis (Dorsey and colleagues) reports that trichloroethylene (TCE) was first linked to parkinsonism in 1969, that four case studies involving eight individuals have linked occupational exposure to TCE to PD, and that a small epidemiological study associated occupational or hobby exposure with a 500% increased risk; the authors postulate that TCE contributes to the global rise of PD and state that further research is necessary to examine this hypothesis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10041423/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] The Camp Lejeune cohort study found higher odds of PD among veterans stationed at the contaminated base than among Camp Pendleton veterans (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.39–2.07). Exposure concerned water containing TCE and other volatile organic compounds, rather than an isolated TCE exposure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10186205/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] The critical review by Atterling Brolin and colleagues argues that converging epidemiological and experimental evidence supports stronger environmental policy action; this is the review authors’ assessment of causality and prevention, rather than proof that every exposure causes PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11832802/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] A UK paraquat-manufacturing workforce mortality study found no evidence of increased PD mortality (SMR 0.67, 95% CI 0.18–1.72). It assessed death-certificate outcomes rather than incident PD and disclosed Syngenta funding. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8157632/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] In the Global Burden of Disease analysis, 6·1 million (95% uncertainty interval 5·0-7·3) individuals had Parkinson's disease globally in 2016, compared with 2·5 million (2·0-3·0) in 1990; age-standardised prevalence rates increased by 21·7% (95% UI 18·1-25·3) over the same period. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30287051/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Goldman and colleagues’ discordant-twin study associated TCE exposure with PD (OR 6.1, 95 percent CI 1.2–33). The very wide interval makes the effect size imprecise. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366287/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] Xie and colleagues’ 2025 meta-analysis estimated a pooled OR of 1.10 (95 percent CI 1.03–1.17) for PD with each 5 μg/m3 increase in long-term PM2.5 exposure. This is an observational pooled association. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11861764/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] The 2025 Northern Ireland cohort found no adjusted overall association between medium-term PM₂.₅ or NO2 exposure and medication-defined PD onset, but reported a positive PM₂.₅ association in participants under 50. Its findings therefore do not support a uniform association across age groups. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12521372/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] A nationwide Taiwan cohort reported positive associations between air-pollutant exposure and PD incidence that persisted in multipollutant models; this observational result does not establish a universal exposure effect. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12322442/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- [statement] In the same projection, population ageing was the largest contributor to the projected growth in cases, ahead of population growth and changes in prevalence. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11881235/ · keywords: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

## Research summary — Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

PD epidemiology includes a rising global burden (Global Burden of Disease estimates and projections) and potentially modifiable environmental exposures. Observational studies associate paraquat, TCE-containing solvent exposures and some air pollutants with PD, but estimates and causal interpretations vary. Paraquat findings include positive case-control results, null workforce mortality evidence and a qualified EPA assessment finding no clear link for labeled uses. TCE evidence includes a small twin study and the mixed-exposure Camp Lejeune cohort. Air-pollution evidence includes positive pooled and Taiwanese results alongside an adjusted overall null Northern Ireland result. Forecasts, odds ratios, exposure mixtures and study outcomes require separate interpretation.

## Source disagreement — Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

Tanner et al. reported increased PD odds with paraquat; EPA states that it has not found a clear link for labeled uses. A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis described a positive association without an indisputable causal conclusion.

## Source disagreement — Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

The air-pollution meta-analysis and Taiwanese cohort report positive associations, whereas Northern Ireland reports an adjusted overall null association with a younger-subgroup exception; exposure duration, population and outcome definitions differ.
